PART FOUR
Relationships & Family
CHAPTER 31
When You Are in Conflict
You agree about the practical matter, but the conversation still
ends badly. Or you settle one argument and find yourselves
having it again a week later, with different details. Something
important has not yet been heard.
Conflict can also begin with a difference that neither person
needs to apologize for. You want different things, remember an
agreement differently, or disagree about what a shared
responsibility requires. The difficulty is finding a way to speak
about it without making the relationship itself feel threatened.
Jesus calls peacemakers blessed:
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of
God.
Matthew 5:9, Berean Standard Bible
Making peace involves work. It can require naming a
disagreement that has been concealed by politeness, or allowing
someone else to explain a concern you had dismissed. The aim is
a relationship in which truth can be spoken and people treated
with care.

154
What remains unsettled?
Before arranging another conversation, consider what you are
actually asking the other person to understand. Is it a decision
you want reconsidered? A promise that has not been kept? A
way of speaking that leaves you reluctant to contribute?
The answer may be different from the subject of the last
argument. A discussion about who will make a call can become a
dispute about whether your time matters. If so, explain that
concern without assuming the other person already knows what
the task represents to you.
Give their concern the same chance to become clear. Philippians
2:3–4 joins humility with attention to other people's interests.
Paul addresses a community whose shared life matters to him;
later in the letter, he appeals to two named women to agree in
the Lord.
Listening from that posture might reveal a responsibility you
have overlooked. It might also confirm that your needs have
been neglected. Humility asks you to take another person
seriously while speaking truthfully about your own situation.
You do not have to invent a fault in yourself to make the
conversation seem balanced. A disagreement can involve
contributions from both people; a wrong can also be one
person's responsibility. Be willing to acknowledge your part
where there is one.
The meeting Jacob feared
Genesis 32:6–21; 33:1–17
Jacob had deceived his father and taken the blessing intended
for Esau. Esau had threatened to kill him, and Jacob had left
home. When the brothers were to meet again years later, Jacob
heard that Esau was coming with four hundred men. He was
afraid.

155
Jacob prayed for deliverance and sent gifts ahead. When he
approached Esau, he bowed to the ground repeatedly. Esau ran
to meet him, embraced him, and kissed him. Both brothers
wept.
After their embrace, the brothers still had decisions to make
about the journey. Esau proposed traveling together; Jacob
spoke of the needs of the children and animals. The narrative
eventually follows them toward different places.
Jacob prepared for hostility and received an embrace. As you
prepare for a conversation, consider which response you are
expecting. Is there room to listen if the person answers
differently?
Sometimes the next workable agreement will be limited. You
might understand one another better without agreeing about
the original decision. You might establish a fair arrangement
while recognizing that closeness will take longer. Such an
outcome can still be worth pursuing.
Choose a conversation that can be useful
In Matthew 18:15–17, Jesus speaks about responding to sin
within the community of His followers. The first approach is
private, with further involvement if the person will not listen.
The passage takes a wrong seriously while seeking to regain the
person.
For an ordinary disagreement, there can be wisdom in speaking
with the person rather than first gathering an audience. Ask
whether this is a suitable time, and keep the first conversation
focused enough to hear a response. An entire history of
grievances may be more than either person can address at once.
You could begin with a question: "I think we understood that
arrangement differently. Could we go back over what each of us
expected?" If a wrong has occurred, name it clearly. Speaking
about your experience need not make the event itself vague.

156
Try to listen long enough to give a fair account of what the other
person means. Then say where you agree and where the
difficulty remains. You may need to pause and return to it,
especially if the exchange has become a contest over who gets to
finish a sentence.
Where there are threats, abuse, or fear of harm, seek support
suited to that situation rather than arranging a private
confrontation. Matthew 18 should not be used to isolate
someone with the person harming them or to prevent
appropriate reporting. Advice about an ordinary disagreement
cannot carry the whole responsibility of responding to abuse.
Leave room for an unfinished result
Psalm 120 ends with a speaker who wants peace among people
who do not. Scripture makes room for the distress of an attempt
that is not received. Romans 12:18 likewise recognizes the limits
of what depends on one person.
After a conversation, consider what has actually changed. Was
something clarified? Is there an agreement to try? Is a further
conversation needed with someone able to help? Keep the next
step proportionate to what you learned.
You can bring an unfinished exchange to God without
rehearsing a final speech that will force agreement. Ask for
patience about what remains open and honesty about anything
you still need to address.
If someone you care about is in conflict
Ask whether they want you to listen or help them prepare for a
conversation. Avoid volunteering to carry messages between
the people involved. If they ask you to take part, be clear about
the role they want and whether it would be appropriate.
Do not make a quick reunion the condition of your support. You
can encourage a fair hearing while recognizing that a peaceful

157
outcome may require changed arrangements or distance. If the
situation involves abuse, help them reach appropriate support
rather than trying to mediate it yourself.
Pause and reflect
What is the concern beneath the subject of the latest argument?
What do you need to understand before asking the other person
to reconsider?
What would a useful, realistic outcome of the next conversation
look like?
A prayer
Lord, help me seek a peace that can bear the truth. Show me what I
need to acknowledge and what I need to hear. Give me words that
explain the concern without attacking the person. Guide us toward
an arrangement we can honor, and help me respond wisely if
agreement remains difficult. In Jesus' name, amen.
For further reading: Matthew 5:9; Philippians 2:1–5; 4:2–3; Genesis 27:30–45; 32:6–21;
33:1–17; Matthew 18:15–17; Psalm 120:6–7; Romans 12:18.
Read also:
• When Forgiving Someone Is Difficult (p. 158), if a particular injury lies beneath the
conflict.
• Asking for Forgiveness (p. 163), if you need to take responsibility for harm you
caused.
• When You Feel Angry (p. 33), if you need space to consider your response before
continuing the discussion.
